parsed_answer.content:
Prior to Java 8, the HashMap implementation relied exclusively on a linked-list structure for handling hash collisions. When multiple keys mapped to the same bucket (a scenario known as a collision), the map would append the new entry to a linked list. In the worst-case scenario—where a malicious actor or poor hash function distribution causes all keys to land in the same bucket—the lookup complexity degrades to O(n). This vulnerability was a significant vector for Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, as an attacker could flood a server with keys that force the JVM to perform linear scans on massive linked lists.

Java 8 introduced a structural transformation to address this: the transition from linked lists to balanced Red-Black trees. This mechanism is triggered by the 'treeify threshold' (a constant value of 8). When a bin contains more than 8 elements, the HashMap converts the linked list into a tree structure. This shift ensures that even in the event of high collision density, the worst-case lookup time complexity is improved to O(log n), providing a robust defense against performance degradation and algorithmic complexity attacks.

items: The TREEIFY_THRESHOLD is set to 8; if a bin exceeds this count, the bin is converted to a tree, provided the total table capacity is at least 64 (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY).
The UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD is set to 6; if a resize operation shrinks the bin count below this value, the tree is converted back into a linked list to save memory.
TreeNode objects are significantly larger than standard Node objects due to the additional pointers required for the tree structure (parent, left, right, prev, and red/black color flag).
The hash calculation for keys remains identical, but the internal bin traversal logic now uses 'instanceof' checks to determine whether to perform a linear list search or a tree-based search.

parsed_answer.content: Senior engineers often overlook that the treeification process is not just about the threshold of 8; the MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64) is a critical guardrail. If your HashMap is small, it will resize rather than treeify, even if you have many collisions. Furthermore, if you implement a custom class as a HashMap key, ensure your hashCode() method is high-quality. While O(log n) is better than O(n), it is still significantly slower than the O(1) performance of a well-distributed hash table. Relying on the tree structure to 'fix' a poor hash function is a performance anti-pattern.

title: What changes were made to HashMap in Java 8? (Treeify threshold, O(log n) lookup)
